name: Gaines Farmhouse

dates.altered: Bought in 2012 and renovated over about a year and a half; a two-bedroom house was opened out on the main floor to house a family of seven (Country Living).

refs.title: See Chip and Joanna Gaines's Farmhouse Up Close and Personal - Country Living
refs.note: 'Their 1,700-square-foot Victorian home sits on 40 beautiful acres in Crawford, Texas, a suburb of Waco ... When the couple purchased their 1895 farmhouse in 2012, they (of course!) chose a fixer upper to update with classic country charm. The whole project took about a year and a half, but the home was worth the wait: What started of as a two-bedroom property now accommodates the seven-person family with an open layout on the main floor.'

refs.title: Chip and Joanna Gaines' "Fixer Upper" Farmhouse - Hooked on Houses
refs.note: 'They live on Magnolia Farm in a farmhouse built in 1895 on the outskirts of Waco, Texas. We watched them fix it up on the first season.'

refs.title: 72 Hours in Joanna Gaines's Waco - Architectural Digest
refs.note: Refers to 'Joanna Gaines's farmhouse in the tiny town of Crawford, Texas, 40-acre sprawl'.

note: THE PHOTOGRAPH THE STYLE IS NAMED AFTER, AND IT IS AN 1895 HOUSE. That is the finding, and it is not a small one for a node whose whole argument is about five dimensions of new construction: the building that transmitted the idiom to a national audience is a nineteenth-century Texas farmhouse of 1,700 square feet, with the pitch, the eave and the porch a nineteenth-century farmhouse has, restored rather than designed. Everything the node lists as the market version's five failures -- flattened pitch, boxed eave, plate-set window head, five-foot entry shed, contrast standing in for depth -- is a deviation from THIS building, made by builders quoting a photograph of it. No dimension beyond the floor area was found; no survey, no listing, and no address is recorded here because it is a private house and the town is what the sources give.
